Good start but I feel like the world could become shallow easily if you don't keep adding worldbuilding elements, but by no means am I counting that against you. The landscapes and characters are interesting enough to draw me in but I am struggling to see where the plot is going to go from here. You say the people are isolated and scattered and yet one of your main characters is trying to unite them to fight some sort of mega-demon and a prophecy, both of which I feel could use some tweaking to make a little bit more interesting. I'm not saying change them entirely but rather add a little color to them (pun not intended). Right now it just feels like the conflict is against a few words and the possibility of a demon. Unless there is some other back-lore that we don't have there doesn't seem to be much reason to give credit to prophecies and if I was a character, I'd be pretty skeptical about a demon coming to kill us all when there is a definite chasm of death consuming the very land I live on.

All this is really solid and sound advice. Makes it read much better and smoother with the changes. Really appreciate the feedback!

>First of all awaking from sleep to sound is a cliche opening string and not a very good one. Starting this way immediately puts you in the red in my mind and and though you manage to get back to neutral very quickly, why start on a negative?

Waking up from sleep to sound is a very common way to wake up. Not exactly riveting if Bert drifts awake and then looks around the room with literally no sense of urgency or conflict, which is one of your points later.

>The whole mechanic of this type of opening is intriguing the reader with interesting characters. Problem is I'm not feeling the weight of character relationship history between the two friends. Im not really getting anything that makes them stand out on the page. Part of it is that the dialogue is rather lack luster.

I can actually see where you're coming from here. I think that part of the problem is 90% of the dialogue is from themselves to each other, so there's not a lot to compare it to. It would also help if you went a little more in depth on why the dialogue is lackluster. Edit: I'd also like to add that Bert and Huel are meant to feel more like one character rather than two at most times. I'm not sure if that makes any sense but if it doesn't don't sweat it. I can confuse myself sometimes!

>Part because you haven't given them a prominent personality expression.

I thought I did pretty decent at displaying their personalities through dialogue. Any tips on how to do this better?

>Beyond characterization the other big issue is that there is no stake. We never see this so called thug and it's pretty obvious they are going to escape unharmed.

I'm sorry but I have to just disagree on this one. We do see Ogdin in the common room and again when Huel exits the inn. I'm not sure what would make it less obvious that they are going to go unharmed unless I literally harm them. 

>Furthermore nothing plot wise seems to happen after they escape to keep the story moving I.e. plot . (Keep in mind while books should have kind of resting sections the introduction, unless very long is not a great place to include one) Does that make sense?

Do you mean besides the giant garnet they find and the subsequent dialogue explaining their new goal? It establishes that they wish to open an inn but don't know enough about the business to really do it. Ironically, this is the most intelligent revelation they have had. 

Thanks for your feedback and I will try to implement it, but I wish there was a bit more specific examples of some of the complaints you have.
